title: Probing The Nature Of Radial Flow: Evidence of its collective origin in Pb+Pb collisions with the ATLAS detector
text:
Summary
This presentation reports the first measurement of the transverse-momentum dependence of radial-flow fluctuations, \(v_0(p_T)\), over \(0.5 < p_T < 10\) GeV in Pb+Pb collisions at \(\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=5.02\) TeV with the ATLAS detector. The measurement satisfies three major hallmarks of collectivity: \(p_T\) factorization, long-range correlations in pseudorapidity, and a centrality-independent response shape. Comparisons with hydrodynamic models further demonstrate the sensitivity of \(v_0(p_T)\) to the bulk viscosity of the QGP.

title: Revealing the Bowling-Pin Geometry of Ne via O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions with ATLAS

The 8th International Conference on the Initial Stages of High-Energy Nuclear Collisions (Initial Stages 2025) Taipei, Taiwan · September 11, 2025
Plenary Talk · Presented on behalf of the ATLAS Collaboration.

title: Revealing the Bowling-Pin Geometry of Ne via O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions with ATLAS
text:
Summary
This presentation reported the first ATLAS measurements of azimuthal flow in O+O and Ne+Ne collisions at a nucleon-pair center-of-mass energy of 5.36 TeV. By comparing two light nuclei of similar size but different predicted intrinsic shapes, the measurement uses collective flow as a probe of nuclear geometry.
In the most central collisions, Ne+Ne exhibits approximately 10% larger elliptic flow than O+O while the triangular flow of the two systems remains similar. Together with multi-particle cumulant measurements, these observations provide evidence for the elongated, bowling-pin-like geometry of the neon nucleus. The measured transverse-momentum dependence of the flow harmonics also displays behavior qualitatively similar to that seen in larger heavy-ion systems, supporting a collective origin for the observed anisotropy.

title: What Information Does Differential Radial Flow Carry?
text:
Somadutta Bhatta, Aman Dimri, Jiangyong Jia
Nuclear Science and Techniques 37, 163 (2026)

title: What Information Does Differential Radial Flow Carry?
text:
Overview
The differential radial-flow observable \(v_0(p_T)\) characterizes event-by-event fluctuations of the transverse-momentum spectrum. Its characteristic shape contains information about radial-flow dynamics, but the observable is also affected by global event-activity and multiplicity fluctuations.
This project asks a basic interpretational question: which features of \(v_0(p_T)\) are actually physical?
Using HIJING simulations, the study shows that changing the definition of event activity or the normalization of the particle spectrum can shift the entire \(v_0(p_T)\) curve vertically. Crucially, these changes leave the shape of the curve essentially unchanged. The absolute vertical position, and therefore the location where \(v_0(p_T)\) crosses zero, is consequently not a robust measure of radial-flow dynamics.

title: What Information Does Differential Radial Flow Carry?
text:
Global Multiplicity and Spectral-Shape Fluctuations
Event-by-event fluctuations of a particle spectrum contain more than one contribution. The total number of particles in an event can fluctuate, while the shape of the transverse-momentum distribution can fluctuate independently.
The observable \(v_0(p_T)\) is sensitive to both effects. Residual fluctuations in event volume or centrality therefore introduce a global contribution that shifts \(v_0(p_T)\) approximately uniformly as a function of \(p_T\).
This means that two measurements can describe the same underlying spectral-shape fluctuations while appearing vertically displaced from one another.

title: What Information Does Differential Radial Flow Carry?
section: Why the Zero Crossing Is Not Physical
text:
Why the Zero Crossing Is Not Physical
A commonly noted feature of \(v_0(p_T)\) is the momentum at which it changes sign. This zero-crossing point often lies near the event-averaged transverse momentum and can appear to provide a characteristic momentum scale.
However, the study demonstrates that the zero crossing moves when the event-activity definition or spectrum-normalization prescription is changed. Since these procedural choices do not alter the underlying radial-flow dynamics, the zero-crossing position cannot by itself carry unique physical information.
Instead, it partly reflects the arbitrary baseline introduced by global multiplicity fluctuations.

title: What Information Does Differential Radial Flow Carry?
section: The Shape Is the Robust Observable
text:
The Shape Is the Robust Observable
While different analysis choices generate an approximately constant vertical offset, the \(p_T\) dependence of \(v_0(p_T)\) remains stable.
The physically meaningful information is therefore encoded in the shape of the differential radial-flow response, or equivalently in its derivative,
\[
\frac{d v_0(p_T)}{d p_T}.
\]
Quantities based on the slope or relative variation of \(v_0(p_T)\) are insensitive to a constant vertical shift and therefore provide a more robust connection to the underlying radial-flow dynamics.

title: What Information Does Differential Radial Flow Carry?
text:
Implications for Experimental Comparisons
This result has a practical consequence for comparisons between experiments and between data and theoretical calculations.
Measurements using different centrality estimators, detector acceptances, or normalization conventions may acquire different vertical offsets even when they contain the same underlying dynamical information. Directly comparing the absolute value or zero crossing of \(v_0(p_T)\) can therefore be misleading.
Instead, measurements should first be vertically aligned, or compared through shape-sensitive quantities. This removes the normalization ambiguity and allows the differential radial-flow response to be used more reliably when constraining properties of the quark-gluon plasma.

title: What Information Does Differential Radial Flow Carry?
section: Connection to the ATLAS Radial-Flow Measurement
text:
Connection to the ATLAS Radial-Flow Measurement
This study complements the experimental measurement establishing the collective nature of differential radial-flow fluctuations. The ATLAS measurement demonstrates that \(v_0(p_T)\) exhibits the characteristic signatures of collectivity, while this work clarifies which features of the observable provide robust dynamical information.

Oral presentation in the Mini-Symposium: The Initial State of Heavy-Ion Collisions I.

title: Probing Effect of Nuclear Shape Coexistence in Heavy-Ion Collisions using Glauber Model
text:
Summary
Nuclear deformation can influence both the initial geometry and final-state observables in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. This presentation explored an additional aspect of nuclear structure: shape coexistence, in which a nucleus can exhibit multiple competing geometric configurations.
Using a Glauber-model description of the collision geometry, the study investigated how shape coexistence modifies initial-state observables relevant for heavy-ion collisions, including eccentricity and transverse-area fluctuations. The work provided an early step toward connecting nuclear-structure information from low-energy measurements with observables accessible in relativistic nuclear collisions.

title: Impact of Nuclear Shape Fluctuations in High-Energy Heavy-Ion Collisions
text:
Aman Dimri, Somadutta Bhatta, Jiangyong Jia
The European Physical Journal A 59, 45 (2023)

title: Impact of Nuclear Shape Fluctuations in High-Energy Heavy-Ion Collisions
text:
Overview
The geometry of an atomic nucleus is commonly characterized by deformation parameters describing its average shape. However, the nuclear shape itself can fluctuate around this average configuration. This project investigates how such fluctuations propagate into the initial geometry of high-energy heavy-ion collisions.
The study focuses on two important initial-state quantities: the eccentricity \(\varepsilon_2\), which is closely connected to elliptic flow, and the inverse transverse size \(d_\perp\), which is related to fluctuations of radial flow. By varying both the magnitude of the quadrupole deformation and its triaxiality, the work explores how fluctuating nuclear structure modifies the event-by-event distributions of these observables.

title: Impact of Nuclear Shape Fluctuations in High-Energy Heavy-Ion Collisions
text:
Nuclear Shape Fluctuations
A quadrupole-deformed nucleus is usually described in terms of an overall deformation magnitude and a triaxiality parameter. Rather than treating these quantities as fixed, this work considers the possibility that they fluctuate from event to event around their mean values.
These fluctuations introduce an additional source of variation in the geometry of the colliding nuclei. Heavy-ion collisions therefore provide a way to study not only the average nuclear shape, but also fluctuations around that average configuration.

title: Impact of Nuclear Shape Fluctuations in High-Energy Heavy-Ion Collisions
text:
Impact on the Initial State
Fluctuations in the overall quadrupole deformation enhance the variances of both \(\varepsilon_2\) and \(d_\perp\) and modify the higher moments of their distributions, including the skewness and kurtosis.
Fluctuations in triaxiality have a qualitatively different effect. They reduce the difference between observables obtained from prolate and oblate nuclear configurations. In the limit of large triaxiality fluctuations, the resulting observables approach those obtained from collisions involving rigid triaxial nuclei.
These behaviors provide a systematic connection between fluctuations of the intrinsic nuclear shape and experimentally accessible fluctuations of collective flow.

title: Impact of Nuclear Shape Fluctuations in High-Energy Heavy-Ion Collisions
text:
Broader Implications
The results illustrate how high-energy nuclear collisions can provide information about nuclear structure that is complementary to conventional low-energy measurements. In particular, the study discusses how the mean quadrupole deformation and fluctuations around that mean may be disentangled through suitable combinations of heavy-ion observables.
This connection between nuclear structure and heavy-ion phenomenology has since become an important part of the broader program of using relativistic collisions to probe the shape and fluctuations of atomic nuclei.

title: Effect of Nuclear Shape Parameters On Initial State Observables In Heavy Ion Collisions
text:
Summary
The initial geometry of a heavy-ion collision is influenced by several properties of the colliding nuclei, including quadrupole deformation, triaxiality, nuclear radius, and skin depth. This poster examined how variations and fluctuations of these nuclear-shape parameters modify observables related to elliptic and radial flow.
The study focused on the initial-state eccentricity and inverse transverse size, investigating their dependence on nuclear deformation across different collision systems. The results showed that fluctuations of the quadrupole deformation enhance the fluctuations of these observables, while triaxiality fluctuations reduce the differences between prolate and oblate nuclear configurations.

title: Aman Dimri
text: I study collective phenomena in high-energy nuclear collisions and use them to probe the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. title: Aman Dimri
Aman Dimri
text:
Featured Research

Evidence for the Collective Nature of Radial Flow



Radial flow characterizes the outward expansion of the quark-gluon plasma produced in heavy-ion collisions. My recent work with the ATLAS Collaboration provided evidence for the collective nature of radial-flow fluctuations through the first measurement of the differential observable \(v_0(p_T)\) in high-energy Pb+Pb collisions at a nucleon-pair center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV.


The observed long-range correlations, transverse-momentum factorization, and centrality-independent response shape provide complementary signatures of a collective origin for radial-flow fluctuations. Comparison with hydrodynamic calculations further revealed a distinctive sensitivity of the measured \(v_0(p_T)\) shape to the bulk viscosity of the quark-gluon plasma.

title: Probing Effect of Nuclear Shape Coexistence in Heavy-Ion Collisions using Glauber Model

Summary
Nuclear geometry can exhibit fluctuations beyond a fixed average deformation, including shape coexistence between competing nuclear configurations. This poster investigated how such shape fluctuations influence the initial geometry of high-energy heavy-ion collisions.
Using a Glauber Monte Carlo model, the study examined the effect of nuclear shape coexistence on observables including eccentricity and transverse-area fluctuations. title: Nuclear Shape Fluctuations in Heavy-Ion Collisions
text:
Summary
Nuclear deformation influences the geometry of the initial state created in heavy-ion collisions. This presentation explored what happens when the nuclear shape itself is allowed to fluctuate from event to event, rather than being described by fixed deformation parameters.
Using analytical estimates and Glauber-model calculations, the study examined fluctuations of the quadrupole deformation magnitude and triaxiality and their impact on initial-state observables related to the shape and transverse size of the collision system. Particular attention was given to how these nuclear-shape fluctuations modify the moments and correlations of the eccentricity and inverse transverse size.
The results illustrate how high-energy heavy-ion collisions can provide sensitivity not only to the average deformation of a nucleus, but also to fluctuations around its equilibrium shape, providing a connection between nuclear-structure physics and experimentally accessible collective observables.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
Aman Dimri, Somadutta Bhatta, and Jiangyong Jia
Quark Matter 2025
Frankfurt am Main, Germany · April 2025

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
Overview
This poster presented a differential view of radial-flow fluctuations using the observable \(v_0(p_T)\). While earlier work had already established the collective nature of radial flow in Pb+Pb collisions, this poster focused on two specific issues that are essential for interpreting the measurement: the role of non-flow contamination and the impact of multiplicity fluctuations.
The goal was to understand which observed features of the differential observable arise from genuine collective dynamics and which may instead reflect biases from particle production or short-range correlations.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
The Differential Observable
Radial flow is commonly quantified through event-by-event fluctuations of the mean transverse momentum, \([p_T]\). A differential version of this idea probes how fluctuations in the local particle spectrum at a given \(p_T\) are correlated with fluctuations in the event-wise radial-flow signal.
The poster discussed two related formulations of differential radial flow:

\(v_0(p_T)\), based on the normalized spectrum \(n(p_T)\),
\(v_0'(p_T)\), based on the full spectrum \(N(p_T)\).

These two constructions are closely related, but they do not respond in the same way to multiplicity fluctuations. Their difference therefore provides a useful handle on the underlying particle-production dynamics.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
What the Poster Examined
The poster focused on two physics questions.
First, it examined whether characteristic features seen in the measured \(v_0(p_T)\) could be influenced by non-flow effects, especially at high \(p_T\). For this purpose, HIJING was used as a non-collective baseline model.
Second, it studied how global multiplicity fluctuations modify the differential observable, and how the comparison between \(v_0(p_T)\) and \(v_0'(p_T)\) can be used to isolate that contribution.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
Impact of Non-Flow Bias
A central point of the poster was that the behavior of \(v_0(p_T)\) in HIJING differs qualitatively from the collective expectation.
In particular:

the factorization behavior is broken in HIJING,
the result depends on the choice of the reference \(p_T\) range,
and \(v_0(p_T)\) rises approximately linearly at high \(p_T\).

These observations support the interpretation that some of the splitting behavior and the strong rise at large \(p_T\) seen in peripheral data are likely influenced by non-flow contamination rather than pure collective radial flow.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
Impact of Multiplicity Fluctuations
The second major message was that \(v_0(p_T)\) itself is comparatively stable across different event ensembles, while \(v_0'(p_T)\) is more sensitive to multiplicity fluctuations.
This makes the difference
\[
v_0'(p_T) - v_0(p_T)
\]
a useful diagnostic quantity. The poster showed that this difference is approximately constant in \(p_T\), consistent with the expectation that it isolates the contribution from multiplicity fluctuations.
This provides a new way to constrain fluctuations in the particle-production process, especially when varying the event classifier or rapidity interval.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
Main Takeaways
The poster highlighted two main conclusions:

some features of the measured differential radial-flow signal, especially the splitting behavior and the large-\(p_T\) rise in peripheral events, can be attributed to non-flow contamination;
the difference between the two formulations of differential radial flow can be used to isolate and understand multiplicity fluctuations.

Together, these results sharpen the interpretation of \(v_0(p_T)\) and clarify how this observable can be used as a robust probe of collective dynamics.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
Relation to the Publication
This poster should be viewed as a companion presentation to the project
“The shape of differential radial flow \(v_0(p_T)\), not its zero-crossing, carries physical information”
Nuclear Science and Techniques 37, 163 (2026).
While the publication develops the main physical interpretation of the differential radial-flow observable, this poster emphasized two additional practical aspects: how to identify non-flow contributions and how to use the difference between alternative definitions to probe multiplicity fluctuations.

title: Revealing Nuclear Geometry with O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions
text:
ATLAS Collaboration
Physical Review C 113, 045205 (2026)

title: Revealing Nuclear Geometry with O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions
text:
Overview
High-energy collisions of light nuclei provide a particularly clean way to study how nuclear geometry is translated into collective motion. In 2025, the LHC delivered oxygen–oxygen and neon–neon collisions at a nucleon-pair center-of-mass energy of 5.36 TeV, allowing ATLAS to compare two systems of similar size but with markedly different predicted nuclear shapes.
The key observable is anisotropic flow, quantified through the coefficients \(v_n\). These coefficients describe angular modulations in the particles produced after the collision and retain information about the geometry of the initial overlap region.
Because oxygen and neon have similar masses, many effects associated simply with system size are reduced in their comparison. This makes differences between the two systems especially sensitive to the underlying nuclear structure.

title: Revealing Nuclear Geometry with O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions
text:
Bowling Balls and Bowling Pins
Nuclear-structure calculations predict that \(^{20}\)Ne has a pronounced prolate deformation, giving it an elongated, bowling-pin-like shape. By contrast, \(^{16}\)O is expected to have a much less elongated geometry.
In the most central collisions, where geometry associated with the impact parameter is minimized, the intrinsic shape of the colliding nuclei becomes particularly important. ATLAS observes a clear enhancement of elliptic flow, \(v_2\), in Ne+Ne relative to O+O collisions. This behavior is consistent with the larger intrinsic deformation expected for neon. The official ATLAS Physics Briefing describes this result as the experimental confirmation of neon’s elongated, “bowling pin” geometry.

title: Revealing Nuclear Geometry with O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions
text:
Measuring the Collective Response
The analysis measures the anisotropic-flow coefficients \(v_2\), \(v_3\), and \(v_4\) as functions of transverse momentum, collision centrality, and event multiplicity.
Two complementary techniques are used. Two-particle correlations provide precise measurements of the flow harmonics after suppressing short-range non-flow contributions, while four-particle subevent cumulants provide additional sensitivity to event-by-event flow fluctuations.
The measurements show the characteristic hierarchy
\[
v_2 > v_3 > v_4,
\]
together with a non-monotonic transverse-momentum dependence similar to that observed in larger heavy-ion systems. These features demonstrate that collective behavior remains prominent even in these much smaller collision systems.

title: Revealing Nuclear Geometry with O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions
text:
Sensitivity to Nuclear Structure
The strongest nuclear-structure signature appears in the comparison between O+O and Ne+Ne collisions.
In central events, \(v_2\) is significantly larger in Ne+Ne collisions than in O+O collisions, consistent with the predicted prolate deformation of \(^{20}\)Ne. Measurements using four-particle cumulants further expose strong event-by-event fluctuations and provide enhanced sensitivity to differences in the underlying nuclear geometry.
By comparing two nuclei of similar mass, the measurement reduces many common systematic and dynamical effects. The remaining differences therefore provide a comparatively clean probe of how intrinsic nuclear geometry is converted into final-state collective flow.

title: Revealing Nuclear Geometry with O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions
text:
Broader Implications
These measurements connect two traditionally distinct areas of nuclear physics: the structure of atomic nuclei and the dynamical evolution of the quark-gluon plasma.
The results provide new experimental constraints on models of light-nucleus structure while simultaneously testing the hydrodynamic response of small collision systems. They also demonstrate how relativistic nuclear collisions can act as an imaging tool, revealing properties of nuclei on timescales far shorter than those accessible through conventional nuclear-structure measurements.
The O+O and Ne+Ne program therefore provides a new laboratory for studying both the emergence of collectivity and the geometry of light nuclei.

title: Evidence for the Collective Nature of Radial Flow
text:
ATLAS Collaboration
Physical Review Letters 136, 032301 (2026)

title: Evidence for the Collective Nature of Radial Flow
text:
Overview
Radial flow is one of the fundamental manifestations of the collective expansion of the quark–gluon plasma (QGP). While anisotropic flow has been extensively established as a collective phenomenon and developed into a precision probe of QGP properties, comparable direct experimental evidence for the global collective nature of radial flow had been missing. This work introduces the first measurement of the transverse-momentum dependence of radial-flow fluctuations, \(v_0(p_T)\), over \(0.5 < p_T < 10\) GeV in Pb+Pb collisions at \(\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=5.02\) TeV with the ATLAS detector. The measurement tests radial flow against three characteristic hallmarks of collectivity: long-range correlations in pseudorapidity, factorization in \(p_T\), and a centrality-independent response shape. All three are observed in the flow-dominated regime, providing direct experimental evidence for the global collective nature of radial flow. Beyond establishing collectivity, comparisons with hydrodynamic calculations demonstrate that \(v_0(p_T)\) is sensitive to the bulk viscosity of the QGP. The measurement therefore establishes differential radial flow as a new tool for studying both the collective dynamics and transport properties of the strongly interacting QGP medium.

title: Evidence for the Collective Nature of Radial Flow
text:
Analysis

Why establish radial-flow collectivity?
The collective expansion of the quark–gluon plasma can manifest itself through two complementary forms of flow. Anisotropic flow reflects the hydrodynamic response to the initial spatial shape of the collision, while radial flow reflects the response to fluctuations in the transverse size and density of the system.
For anisotropic flow, its collective origin has been established experimentally through a broad set of characteristic signatures, including long-range correlations, factorization, and a universal hydrodynamic response. Radial flow, despite being of comparable fundamental importance, had not been subjected to the same direct experimental tests.
This distinction matters because radial-flow observables are increasingly being used to constrain properties of the QGP. Event-by-event fluctuations of the mean transverse momentum, \([p_T]\), exhibit striking behavior in ultra-central Pb+Pb collisions, including a sharp suppression of their variance and a rapid increase of \(\langle[p_T]\rangle\) with multiplicity. These features have been interpreted within a hydrodynamic picture in which radial-flow fluctuations originate from both global collision geometry and local density fluctuations.
Before such observables can be used as precision probes of the QGP equation of state or transport properties, however, an important logical step must be established experimentally: is radial flow itself genuinely collective?


Differential radial flow
To answer this question, the analysis introduces the differential radial-flow observable \(v_0(p_T)\).
Its physical origin can be understood by considering events with approximately fixed total entropy. An event with a smaller transverse collision area develops stronger pressure gradients and therefore experiences a larger radial push. Its particle spectrum becomes flatter and its event-by-event mean transverse momentum \([p_T]\) increases. Conversely, an event with a larger transverse area experiences weaker radial expansion and develops a steeper spectrum.
This produces a characteristic correlation between fluctuations of the local particle yield and fluctuations of \([p_T]\). At low \(p_T\), the two quantities are anticorrelated; near the ensemble mean transverse momentum the correlation crosses zero; and at higher \(p_T\) it becomes positive.
The differential observable is constructed from this correlation,
\[
v_0(p_T)
=
\frac{1}{v_0}
\frac{
\langle \delta n(p_T)\delta[p_T]\rangle
}{
\langle n(p_T)\rangle\langle[p_T]\rangle
},
\]
where \(n(p_T)\) is the normalized particle spectrum and \(v_0\) is the corresponding integrated radial-flow fluctuation.






Figure 1: Schematic illustration of the physical origin of differential radial flow. Events with larger \([p_T]\) have flatter spectra, while events with smaller \([p_T]\) have steeper spectra, producing a characteristic sign change in the correlation between \(\delta n(p_T)\) and \(\delta[p_T]\).



A two-subevent method is used in which the local spectrum and \([p_T]\) are measured using particles separated in pseudorapidity. This suppresses short-range correlations and allows the global component of the radial-flow signal to be isolated.


Experimental hallmarks of collectivity
The key idea of the measurement is to test radial flow against the same experimental criteria that are traditionally used to establish anisotropic collectivity.

Long-range correlations
A global collective expansion should generate correlations extending over large separations in pseudorapidity. Experimentally, \(v_0(p_T)\) is found to be largely insensitive to the pseudorapidity gap used between the two subevents, as shown in Figure 2.






Figure 2: Differential radial flow \(v_0(p_T)\) measured for different pseudorapidity gaps in central and peripheral Pb+Pb collisions. The weak dependence on the gap size demonstrates the long-range nature of the radial-flow correlation.



This behavior is observed in both central and peripheral Pb+Pb collisions. Deviations appear primarily at larger \(p_T\), where contributions from jets and other non-flow effects become increasingly important.


Centrality-independent response
The absolute magnitude of \(v_0(p_T)\) varies strongly with collision centrality. Much of this variation reflects changes in the magnitude of the initial-state size fluctuations rather than changes in the subsequent hydrodynamic response.
To reduce this dependence, the differential measurement is divided by its integrated counterpart, \(v_0\). As shown in Figure 3, the resulting quantity, \(v_0(p_T)/v_0\), exhibits a striking behavior: curves from widely separated centrality intervals collapse onto an approximately common shape in the flow-dominated region.






Figure 3: Differential radial flow \(v_0(p_T)\) for different centrality intervals before and after normalization by the integrated radial-flow fluctuation \(v_0\). The strong centrality dependence of the absolute magnitude is substantially reduced after normalization, revealing an approximately universal response shape in the flow-dominated region.



This centrality-independent shape indicates that very different initial collision geometries are being transformed into momentum space through a common underlying hydrodynamic response.


Factorization
A collective mode generated by a global hydrodynamic expansion is also expected to satisfy factorization. This is tested by changing the reference \(p_T\) interval used to define \([p_T]\) and its event-by-event fluctuations. For \(p_T \lesssim 3\) GeV, the measured \(v_0(p_T)\) is essentially insensitive to this choice, demonstrating factorization in the region dominated by soft collective physics, as shown in Figure 4.






Figure 4: Differential radial flow \(v_0(p_T)\) measured using different reference \(p_T\) ranges in central and peripheral Pb+Pb collisions. The agreement of the measurements at low \(p_T\) demonstrates factorization in the flow-dominated regime.



At larger transverse momentum, the factorization begins to break. In peripheral collisions, this behavior is consistent with increasing contamination from residual non-flow correlations, while in central collisions the high-\(p_T\) response becomes sensitive to jet-quenching phenomena.



Connection to QGP transport properties
Once the collective nature of radial flow is established, the differential observable can be used to investigate properties of the medium itself.
The measured \(v_0(p_T)/v_0\) is compared with hydrodynamic calculations based on the Trento+MUSIC framework. The ideal-hydrodynamic calculation and the calculation including shear viscosity give very similar predictions and underestimate the data at high \(p_T\), failing to reproduce the measured shape. In contrast, the inclusion of a temperature-dependent bulk viscosity, \(\zeta/s(T)\), substantially modifies the high-\(p_T\) behavior and provides a much better description of the data. After additionally accounting for the difference in the mean transverse momentum between model and data by scaling the horizontal axis with \(\bar{p}_T\), the agreement improves further, as shown in Figure 5.






Figure 5: Comparison of the measured scaled differential radial flow with Trento+MUSIC hydrodynamic calculations. The ideal and shear-only calculations underestimate the data at high \(p_T\), while including a temperature-dependent bulk viscosity significantly improves the description. Scaling the horizontal axis by the mean transverse momentum further improves the agreement.



The normalization by the integrated \(v_0\) suppresses much of the influence of the initial-state fluctuation magnitude and emphasizes the hydrodynamic response. The improved description of the measured shape after including bulk viscosity demonstrates the sensitivity of differential radial flow to \(\zeta/s\), establishing \(v_0(p_T)\) as a new experimental probe of QGP transport properties.


Broader implications
By exhibiting long-range correlations, a centrality-independent response shape, and factorization, radial flow satisfies the same key hallmarks of collectivity established for azimuthal flow. These results elevate radial flow to the rigorous standing of azimuthal flow, establishing it as a powerful new probe for constraining QGP transport properties.
The same observable also opens a path toward future system-size studies. Measurements of \(v_0(p_T)\) in systems such as p+O, O+O, Ne+Ne, and other small (p+p) or exotic collision systems (\(\gamma\)+Pb) could provide an independent probe of collectivity, help explore how the emergence of QGP-like behavior evolves with system size, and ultimately help identify the smallest collision systems capable of forming a QGP droplet.

title: About Me
text:
I am a physicist and graduate researcher at Stony Brook University studying the quark-gluon plasma created in high-energy nuclear collisions. My research focuses on collective phenomena and event-by-event fluctuations, with the goal of understanding how the initial geometry of a nuclear collision and the transport properties of the resulting medium are encoded in experimentally measurable momentum correlations.
I am a member of both the ATLAS Collaboration at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN and the STAR Collaboration at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL). My research combines experimental measurements with hydrodynamic calculations and initial-state models to study the connection between collision geometry, fluctuations, and the dynamical response of the quark-gluon plasma.


A central theme of my current work is the study of radial-flow fluctuations. These measurements provide a complementary perspective on collective dynamics and offer new ways to probe the transport properties of the quark-gluon plasma, including its bulk viscosity.
I am also interested in nuclear structure, initial-state fluctuations, system-size dependence, and the emergence of collective behavior across different collision systems.
